entries.0b08e92cad3b44dd80fd008199cfe2aed805671f: <div sID="gen31025" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Cor.2" sID="1Cor.2"/> <div eID="gen31025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31026" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31027" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds with his argument in this chapter, and, I. Reminds the Corinthians of the plain manner wherein he delivered the gospel to them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1-1Cor.2.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. But yet, II. Shows them that he had communicated to them a treasure of the truest and highest wisdom, such as exceeded all the attainments of learned men, such as could never have entered into the heart of man if it had not been revealed, nor can be received and improved to salvation but by the light and influence of that Spirit who revealed it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.16">ver. 6 to the end</reference>.
entries.b02b2e074d2245a448c6306ab8a3e68530a5b801: <div eID="gen31027" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31026" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Ministry. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. <hi type="super">4</hi> And my speech and my preaching <hi type="italic">was</hi> not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: 5 That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. <div eID="gen31028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31029" type="x-p"/> In this passage the apostle pursues his design, and reminds the Corinthians how he acted when he first preached the gospel among them. <div eID="gen31029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31030" type="x-p"/> I. As to the matter or subject he tell us (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">He determined to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ and him crucified</hi>—to make a show of no other knowledge than this, to preach nothing, to discover the knowledge of nothing, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Note, Christ, in his person and offices, is the sum and substance of the gospel, and ought to be the great subject of a gospel minister's preaching. His business is to display the banner of the cross, and invite people under it. Anyone that heard Paul preach found him to harp so continually on this string that he would say he knew nothing but Christ and him crucified. Whatever other knowledge he had, this was the only knowledge he discovered, and showed himself concerned to propagate among his hearers. <div eID="gen31030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31031" type="x-p"/> II. The manner wherein he preached Christ is here also observable. 1. Negatively. <hi type="italic">He came not among them with excellency of speech or wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">His speech and preaching were not with enticing words of man's wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">v. 4</reference>. He did not affect to appear a fine orator or a deep philosopher; nor did he insinuate himself into their minds, by a flourish of words, or a pompous show of deep reason and extraordinary science and skill. He did not set himself to captivate the ear by fine turns and eloquent expressions, nor to please and entertain the fancy with lofty flights of sublime notions. Neither his speech, nor the wisdom he taught, savoured of human skill: he learnt both in another school. Divine wisdom needed not to be set off with such human ornaments. 2. Positively. He came among them <hi type="italic">declaring the testimony of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">v. 1</reference>. He published a divine revelation, and gave in sufficient vouchers for the authority of it, both by its consonancy to ancient predictions and by present miraculous operations; and there he left the matter. Ornaments of speech and philosophical skill and argument could add no weight to what came recommended by such authority. <hi type="italic">He was also among them in weakness and fear, and in much trembling;</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">his speech and preaching were in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.3-1Cor.2.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. His enemies in the church of Corinth spoke very contemptuously of him: <hi type="italic">His bodily presence, say they, is weak, and his speech contemptible,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2 Cor. x. 10</reference>. Possibly he had a little body, and a low voice; but, though he had not so good an elocution as some, it is plain that he was no mean speaker. The men of Lystra looked on him to be the heathen god Mercury, come down to them in the form of a man, because he was the chief speaker, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.12">Acts xiv. 12</reference>. Nor did he want courage nor resolution to go through his work; he was <hi type="italic">in nothing terrified by his adversaries.</hi> Yet he was no boaster. He did not proudly vaunt himself, like his opposers. He acted in his office with much modesty, concern, and care. He behaved with great humility among them; not as one grown vain with the honour and authority conferred on him, but as one concerned to approve himself faithful, and fearful of himself, lest he should mismanage in his trust. Observe, None know the fear and trembling of faithful ministers, who are zealous over souls with a godly jealousy; and a deep sense of their own weakness is the occasion of this fear and trembling. They know how insufficient they are, and are therefore fearful for themselves. But, though Paul managed with this modesty and concern, yet he spoke with authority: <hi type="italic">In the demonstration of the Spirit and of power.</hi> He preached the truths of Christ in their native dress, with plainness of speech. He laid down the doctrine as the Spirit delivered it; and left the Spirit, by his external operation in signs and miracles, and his internal influences on the hearts of men, to demonstrate the truth of it, and procure its reception. <div eID="gen31031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31032" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the end mentioned for which he preached Christ crucified in this manner: <hi type="italic">That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of man, but the power of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.5">v. 5</reference>)—that they might not be drawn by human motives, nor overcome by mere human arguments, lest it should be said that either rhetoric or logic had made them Christians. But, when nothing but Christ crucified was plainly preached, the success must be founded, not on human wisdom, but divine evidence and operation. The gospel was so preached that God might appear and be glorified in all.
entries.61af95647cf3e0c7699087b0eb2a33320046e335: <div eID="gen31032" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Discoveries of the Gospel; Spiritual Things Spiritually Discerned. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: <hi type="super">7</hi> But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the hidden <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> which God ordained before the world unto our glory: <hi type="super">8</hi> Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. <hi type="super">9</hi> But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. <hi type="super">10</hi> But God hath revealed <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God. <hi type="super">11</hi> For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. <hi type="super">13</hi> Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. <hi type="super">14</hi> But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know <hi type="italic">them,</hi> because they are spiritually discerned. <hi type="super">15</hi> But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man. <hi type="super">16</hi> For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ. <div eID="gen31033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31034" type="x-p"/> In this part of the chapter the apostle shows them that though he had not come to them with the excellency of human wisdom, with any of the boasted knowledge and literature of the Jews or Greeks, yet he had communicated to them a treasure of the truest and the highest wisdom: <hi type="italic">We speak wisdom among those who are perfect</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">v. 6</reference>), among those who are well instructed in Christianity, and come to some maturity in the things of God. Those that receive the doctrine as divine, and, having been illuminated by the Holy Spirit, have looked well into it, discover true wisdom in it. They not only understand the plain history of Christ, and him crucified, but discern the deep and admirable designs of the divine wisdom therein. Though what we preach is foolishness to the world, it is wisdom to them. They are made wise by it, and can discern wisdom in it. Note, Those who are wise themselves are the only proper judges of what is wisdom; <hi type="italic">not</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the wisdom of God in a mystery</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.7">v. 6, 7</reference>); not worldly wisdom, but divine; not such as the men of this world could have discovered, nor such as worldly men, under the direction of pride, and passion, and appetite, and worldly interest, and destitute of the Spirit of God, can receive. Note, How different is the judgment of God from that of the world! <hi type="italic">He seeth not as man seeth.</hi> The wisdom he teaches is of a quite different kind from what passes under that notion in the world. It is not the wisdom of politicians, nor philosophers, nor rabbis (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">v. 6</reference>), not such as they teach nor such as they relish; <hi type="italic">but the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom of God</hi>—what he had a long time kept to himself, and concealed from the world, and the depth of which, now it is revealed, none but himself can fathom. <hi type="italic">It is the mystery which hath been hid from ages and generations, though now made manifest to the saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col. i. 26</reference>), hid in a manner entirely from the heathen world, and made mysterious to the Jews, by being wrapped up in dark types and distant prophecies, but revealed and made known to us by the Spirit of God. Note, See the privilege of those who enjoy the gospel revelation: to them types are unveiled, mysteries made plain, prophecies interpreted, and the secret counsels of God published and laid open. The wisdom of God in a mystery is now made manifest to the saints. Now, concerning this wisdom, observe, <div eID="gen31034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31035" type="x-p"/> I. The rise and origin of it: <hi type="italic">It was ordained of God, before the world, to our glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">v. 7</reference>. It was ordained of God; he had determined long ago to reveal and make it known, from many ages past, from the beginning, nay, from eternity; and that to our glory, <hi type="italic">the glory of us,</hi> either us apostles or us Christians. It was a great honour put upon the apostles, to be entrusted with the revelation of this wisdom. It was a great and honourable privilege for Christians to have this glorious wisdom discovered to them. And the wisdom of God discovered to them. And the wisdom of God discovered in the gospel, the divine wisdom taught by the gospel, prepares for our everlasting glory and happiness in the world to come. The counsels of God concerning our redemption are dated from eternity, and designed for the glory and happiness of the saints. And what deep wisdom was in these counsels! Note, The wisdom of God is both employed and displayed for the honour of the saints—employed from eternity, and displayed in time, to make them glorious both here and hereafter, in time and to eternity. What honour does he put on his saints! <div eID="gen31035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31036" type="x-p"/> II. The ignorance of the great men of the world about it: <hi type="italic">Which none of the princes of this world knew</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">v. 8</reference>), the principal men in authority and power, or in wisdom and learning. The Roman governor, and the guides and rulers of the Jewish church and nation, seem to be the persons here chiefly meant. These were the princes of this world, or this age, who, had they known this true and heavenly wisdom, would not have crucified the Lord of glory. This Pilate and the Jewish rulers literally did when our Redeemer was crucified upon the sentence of the one and the clamorous demands of the other. Observe, Jesus Christ is the Lord of Glory, a title much too great for any creature to bear: and the reason why he was hated was because he was not known. Had his crucifiers known him, known who and what he was, they would have withheld their impious hands, and not have taken and slain him. This he pleaded with his Father for their pardon: <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Luke xxiii. 34</reference>. Note, There are many things which people would not do if they knew the wisdom of God in the great work of redemption. They act as they do because they are blind or heedless. They know not the truth, or will not attend to it. <div eID="gen31036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31037" type="x-p"/> III. It is such wisdom as could not have been discovered without a revelation, according to what the prophet Isaiah says (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa. lxiv. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man the things which God hath prepared for those that love him—for him that waiteth for him,</hi> that waiteth for his mercy, so the LXX. It was a testimony of love to God in the Jewish believers to live in expectation of the accomplishment o evangelical promises. Waiting upon God is an evidence of love to him. <hi type="italic">Lo, this is our God, we have waited for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">Isa. xxv. 9</reference>. Observe, There are things which God hath prepared for those that love him, and wait for him. There are such things prepared in a future life for them, things which sense cannot discover, no present information can convey to our ears, nor can yet enter our hearts. <hi type="italic">Life and immortality are brought to light through the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2 Tim. i. 10</reference>. But the apostle speaks here of the subject-matter of the divine revelation under the gospel. These are such as eye hath not seen nor ear heard. Observe, The great truths of the gospel are things lying out of the sphere of human discovery: <hi type="italic">Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard them, nor have they entered into the heart of man.</hi> Were they objects of sense, could they be discovered by an eye of reason, and communicated by the ear to the mind, as matters of common human knowledge may, there had been no need of a revelation. But, lying out of the sphere of nature, we cannot discover them but by the light of revelation. And therefore we must take them as they lie in the scriptures, and as God has been pleased to reveal them. <div eID="gen31037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31038" type="x-p"/> IV. We here see by whom this wisdom is discovered to us: <hi type="italic">God hath revealed them to us by his Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">v. 10</reference>. The scripture is given by inspiration of God. <hi type="italic">Holy men spoke of old as they were moved by the Holy Ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2 Pet. i. 21</reference>. And the apostles spoke by inspiration of the same Spirit, as he taught them, and gave them utterance. Here is a proof of the divine authority of the holy scriptures. Paul wrote what he taught: and what he taught was revealed of God by his Spirit, <hi type="italic">that Spirit that searches all things, yea, the deep things of God, and knows the things of God, as the spirit of a man that is in him knows the things of a man,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">v. 11</reference>. A double argument is drawn from these words in proof of the divinity of the Holy Ghost:—1. Omniscience is attributed to him: <hi type="italic">He searches all things, even the deep things of God.</hi> He has exact knowledge of all things, and enters into the very depths of God, penetrates into his most secret counsels. Now who can have such a thorough knowledge of God but God? 2. This allusion seems to imply that the Holy Spirit is as much in God as a man's mind is in himself. Now the mind of the man is plainly essential to him. He cannot be without his mind. Now can God be without his Spirit. He is as much and as intimately one with God as the man's mind is with the man. The man knows his own mind because his mind is one with himself. The Spirit of God knows the things of God because he is one with God. And as no man can come at the knowledge of what is in another man's mind till he communicates and reveals it, so neither can we know the secret counsels and purposes of God till they are made known to us by his Holy Spirit. We cannot know them at all till he had proposed them objectively (as it is called) in the external revelation; we cannot know or believe them to salvation till he enlightens the faculty, opens the eye of the mind, and gives us such a knowledge and faith of them. And it was by this Spirit that the apostles had received the <hi type="italic">wisdom of God in a mystery,</hi> which they spoke. "<hi type="italic">Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is of God, that we might know the things freely given to us of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">v. 12</reference>); not the spirit which is in the <hi type="italic">wise men of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">v. 6</reference>), nor in the <hi type="italic">rulers of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">v. 8</reference>), but the <hi type="italic">Spirit which is of God,</hi> or proceedeth from God. We have what we deliver in the name of God by inspiration from him; and it is by his gracious illumination and influence that <hi type="italic">we know the things freely given to us of God</hi> unto salvation"—that is, "the great privileges of the gospel, which are the free gift of God, distributions of mere and rich grace." Though these things are given to us, and the revelation of this gift is made to us, we cannot know them to any saving purpose till we have the Spirit. The apostles had the revelation of these things from the Spirit of God, and the saving impression of them from the same Spirit. <div eID="gen31038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31039" type="x-p"/> V. We see here in what manner this wisdom was taught or communicated: <hi type="italic">Which things we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Ghost teaches,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13">v. 13</reference>. They had received the wisdom they taught, not from the wise men of the world, but from the Spirit of God. Nor did they put a human dress on it, but plainly declared the doctrine of Christ, in terms also taught them by the Holy Spirit. He not only gave them the knowledge of these things, but gave them utterance. Observe, The truths of God need no garnishing by human skill or eloquence, but look best in the words which the Holy Ghost teaches. The Spirit of God knows much better how to speak of the things of God than the best critics, orators, or philosophers. <hi type="italic">Comparing spiritual things with spiritual</hi>—one part of revelation with another, the revelation of the gospel with that of the Jews, the discoveries of the New Testament with the types and prophecies of the Old. The comparing of matters of revelation with matters of science, things supernatural with things natural and common, is going by a wrong measure. Spiritual things, when brought together, will help to illustrate one another; but, if the principles of human art and science are to be made a test of revelation, we shall certainly judge amiss concerning it, and the things contained in it. Or, <hi type="italic">adapting spiritual things to spiritual</hi>—speaking of spiritual matters, matters of revelation, and the spiritual life, in language that is proper and plain. The language of the Spirit of God is the most proper to convey his meaning. <div eID="gen31039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31040" type="x-p"/> VI. We have an account how this wisdom is received. <div eID="gen31040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31041" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The natural man receiveth not the things of God, for they are foolishness to him, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">v. 14</reference>. The <hi type="italic">natural man, the animal man.</hi> Either, (1.) The man under the power of corruption, and never yet illuminated by the Spirit of God, such as Jude calls <hi type="italic">sensual, not having the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.19">v. 19</reference>. Men unsanctified receive not the things of God. The understanding, through the corruption of nature by the fall, and through the confirmation of this disorder by customary sin, is utterly unapt to receive the rays of divine light; it is prejudiced against them. The truths of God are foolishness to such a mind. The man looks on them as trifling and impertinent things, not worth his minding. <hi type="italic">The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.5">John i. 5</reference>. Not that the natural faculty of discerning is lost, but evil inclinations and wicked principles render the man unwilling to enter into the mind of God, in the spiritual matters of his kingdom, and yield to their force and power. It is the quickening beams of the Spirit of truth and holiness that must help the mind to discern their excellency, and to so thorough a conviction of their truth as heartily to receive and embrace them. Thus the natural man, the man destitute of the Spirit of God, cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. Or, (2.) The natural man, that is, the wise man of the world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19-1Cor.1.20">ch. i. 19, 20</reference>), the wise man after the flesh, or according to the flesh (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.26">v. 26</reference>), one who hath the wisdom of the world, man's wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4-1Cor.2.6">ch. ii. 4-6</reference>), a man, as some of the ancients, that would learn all truth by his own ratiocinations, receive nothing by faith, nor own any need of supernatural assistance. This was very much the character of the pretenders to philosophy and the Grecian learning and wisdom in that day. Such a man receives not the things of the Spirit of God. Revelation is not with him a principle of science; he looks upon it as delirium and dotage, the extravagant thought of some deluded dreamer. It is no way to wisdom among the famous masters of the world; and for that reason he can have no knowledge of things revealed, because they are only spiritually discerned, or made known by the revelation of the Spirit, which is a principle of science or knowledge that he will not admit. <div eID="gen31041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31042" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged,</hi> or discerned, <hi type="italic">of no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Either, (1.) He who is sanctified and made spiritually-minded (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.6">Rom. viii. 6</reference>) judgeth all things, or discerneth all things—he is capable of judging about matters of human wisdom, and has also a relish and savour of divine truths; he sees divine wisdom, and experiences divine power, in gospel revelations and mysteries, which the carnal and unsanctified mind looks upon as weakness and folly, as things destitute of all power and not worthy any regard. It is the sanctified mind that must discern the real beauties of holiness; but, by the refinement of its facilities, they do not lose their power of discerning and judging about common and natural things. The spiritual man may judge of all things, natural and supernatural, human and divine, the deductions of reason and the discoveries of revelation. But he himself is judged or discerned of <hi type="small-caps">no man</hi> . God's saints are his hidden ones, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Ps. lxxxiii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their life is hid with Christ in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col. iii. 3</reference>. The carnal man knows no more of a spiritual man than he does of other spiritual things. He is a stranger to the principles, pleasures, and actings, of the divine life. The spiritual man does not lie open to his observation. Or, (2.) <hi type="italic">He that is spiritual</hi> (who has had divine revelations made to him, receives them as such, and founds his faith and religion upon them) can judge both of common things and things divine; he can discern what is, and what is not, the doctrine of the gospel and of salvation, and whether a man preaches the truths of God or not. He does not lose the power of reasoning, nor renounce the principles of it, by founding his faith and religion on revelation. But <hi type="italic">he himself is judged of no man</hi>—can be judged, so as to be confuted, by no man; nor can any man who is not spiritual, not under a divine <hi type="italic">afflatus</hi> himself (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.37">ch. xiv. 37</reference>), or not founding his faith on a divine revelation, discern or judge whether what he speaks be true or divine, or not. In short, he who founds all his knowledge upon principles of science, and the mere light of reason, can never be a judge of the truth or falsehood of what is received by revelation. <hi type="italic">For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">v. 16</reference>), that is, the <hi type="italic">spiritual man?</hi> Who can enter so far into the mind of God as to instruct him who has the Spirit of God, and is under his inspiration? He only is the person to whom God immediately communicates the knowledge of his will. And who can inform or instruct him in the mind of God who is so immediately under the conduct of his own Spirit? Very few have known any thing of the mind of God by a natural power. <hi type="italic">But,</hi> adds the apostle, <hi type="italic">we have the mind of Christ;</hi> and the mind of Christ is the mind of God. He is God, and the principal messenger and prophet of God. And the apostles were empowered by his Spirit to make known his mind to us. And in the holy scriptures the mind of Christ, and the mind of God in Christ, are fully revealed to us. Observe, It is the great privilege of Christians that they have the mind of Christ revealed to them by his Spirit.  <chapter eID="1Cor.2"/> <div eID="gen31042" type="x-p"/>

entries.619f7de966f154a97d183b75d5952a15ed3f0316: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16768"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1-1Cor.2.16">1Co 2:1-16</reference>. Paul's Subject of Preaching, Christ Crucified, Not in Worldly, but in Heavenly, Wisdom among the Perfect.<div eID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16768"/><hi type="bold">1. And I--</hi>"So I" [Conybeare] as one of the "foolish, weak, and despised" instruments employed by God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>); "glorying in the Lord," not in man's wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">1Co 1:31</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">1Co 1:23</reference>, "We."<div eID="gen33005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I came--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.18.1">Ac 18:1</reference>, &c.). Paul might, had he pleased, have used an ornate style, having studied secular learning at Tarsus of Cilicia, which Strabo preferred as a school of learning to Athens or Alexandria; here, doubtless, he read the Cilician Aratus' poems (which he quotes, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Ac 17:28</reference>), and Epimenides (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>), and Menander (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>). Grecian intellectual development was an important element in preparing the way for the Gospel, but it failed to regenerate the world, showing that for this a superhuman power is needed. Hellenistic (Grecizing) Judaism at Tarsus and Alexandria was the connecting link between the schools of Athens and those of the Rabbis. No more fitting birthplace could there have been for the apostle of the Gentiles than Tarsus, free as it was from the warping influences of Rome, Alexandria, and Athens. He had at the same time Roman citizenship, which protected him from sudden violence. Again, he was reared in the Hebrew divine law at Jerusalem. Thus, as the three elements, Greek cultivation, Roman polity (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Lu 2:1</reference>), and the divine law given to the Jews, combined just at Christ's time, to prepare the world for the Gospel, so the same three, by God's marvellous providence, met together in the apostle to the Gentiles [Conybeare and Howson].<div eID="gen33006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testimony of God--</hi>"the testimony of Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">1Co 1:6</reference>); therefore Christ is God. <div eID="gen33007" type="x-p"/>
entries.6af1a86eb76fead3ddf1cf7d03ae73d6f5fd9668: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16769"/><div sID="gen33008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16769"/>2. The Greek implies, "The only definite thing that I made it my business to know among you, was to know Jesus Christ (His person) and Him crucified (His office)" [Alford], not exalted on the earthly throne of David, but executed as the vilest malefactor. The historical fact of Christ's crucifixion had probably been put less prominently forward by the seekers after human wisdom in the Corinthian church, to avoid offending learned heathens and Jews. Christ's person and Christ's office constitute the sum of the Gospel. <div eID="gen33008" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbe7608718f4066eefb2ed57158e684504f79331: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16770"/><div sID="gen33009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16770"/><hi type="bold">3. I--</hi>the preacher: as <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1Co 2:2</reference> describes the subject, "Christ crucified," and <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">1Co 2:4</reference> the mode of preaching: "my speech ... not with enticing words," "but in demonstration of the Spirit."<div eID="gen33009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weakness--</hi>personal and bodily (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen33010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trembling--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Php 2:12</reference>). Not personal fear, but a trembling anxiety to perform a duty; anxious conscientiousness, as proved by the contrast to "eye service" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>) [Conybeare and Howson]. <div eID="gen33011" type="x-p"/>
entries.a433486aceb92fe64b201ab04034c7bee8db1bd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16771"/><div sID="gen33012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16771"/><hi type="bold">4. my speech--</hi>in private.<div eID="gen33012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preaching--</hi>in public [Bengel]. Alford explains it, My discourse on doctrines, and my preaching or announcement of facts.<div eID="gen33013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enticing--</hi>rather, "persuasive."<div eID="gen33014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man's wisdom--</hi>man's is omitted in the oldest authorities. Still "wisdom" does refer to "man's" wisdom.<div eID="gen33015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in demonstration of ... Spirit, &c.--</hi>Persuasion is man's means of moving his fellow man. God's means is demonstration, leaving no doubt, and inspiring implicit faith, by the powerful working of the Spirit (then exhibited both outwardly by miracles, and inwardly by working on the heart, now in the latter and the more important way only, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">Mt 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.10">Ac 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>; compare also <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Ro 15:19</reference>). The same simple power accompanies divine truth now, producing certain persuasion and conversion, when the Spirit demonstrates by it. <div eID="gen33016" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b92dfae3ebedaf73909b114ac7d4f997d492cd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16772"/><div sID="gen33017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16772"/><hi type="bold">5. stand in ... wisdom of men--</hi>rest on it, owe its origin and continuance to it. <div eID="gen33017" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4da01b5df2fce656cbfe007a3dcbfec771518b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16773"/><div sID="gen33018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16773"/>6-7. Yet the Gospel preaching, so far from being at variance with true "wisdom," is a wisdom infinitely higher than that of the wise of the world.<div eID="gen33018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we speak--</hi>resuming "we" (preachers, I, Apollos, &c.) from "we preach" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>), only that here, "we speak" refers to something less public (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>, "mystery ... hidden") than "we preach," which is public. For "wisdom" here denotes not the whole of Christian doctrine, but its sublimer and deeper principles.<div eID="gen33019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect--</hi>Those matured in Christian experience and knowledge alone can understand the true superiority of the Christian wisdom which Paul preached. Distinguished not only from worldly and natural men, but also from babes, who though "in Christ" retain much that is "carnal" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Co 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>), and cannot therefore understand the deeper truths of Christianity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">1Co 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">Php 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">He 5:14</reference>). Paul does not mean by the "mystery" or "hidden wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>) some hidden tradition distinct from the Gospel (like the Church of Rome's disciplina arcani and doctrine of reserve), but the unfolding of the treasures of knowledge, once hidden in God's counsels, but now announced to all, which would be intelligently comprehended in proportion as the hearer's inner life became perfectly transformed into the image of Christ. Compare instances of such "mysteries," that is, deeper Christian truths, not preached at Paul's first coming to Corinth, when he confined himself to the fundamental elements (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1Co 2:2</reference>), but now spoken to the "perfect" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">6</reference>). "Perfect" is used not of absolute perfection, but relatively to "babes," or those less ripe in Christian growth (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">Php 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="1John.2.12-1John.2.14">1Jo 2:12-14</reference>). "God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>) is opposed to the world, the apostles to "the princes [great and learned men] of this world" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen33020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to naught--</hi>nothingness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>). They are transient, not immortal. Therefore, their wisdom is not real [Bengel]. Rather, translate with Alford, "Which are being brought to naught," namely, by God's choosing the "things which are not (the weak and despised things of the Gospel), to bring to naught (the same verb as here) things that are" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>). <div eID="gen33021" type="x-p"/>
entries.39b83601b4d4135c81fb409634919ef9d2206184: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16775"/><div sID="gen33027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16775"/><hi type="bold">8. Which--</hi>wisdom. The strongest proof of the natural man's destitution of heavenly wisdom.<div eID="gen33027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crucified ... Lord of glory--</hi>implying the inseparable connection of Christ's humanity and His divinity. The Lord of glory (which He had in His own right before the world was, <reference osisRef="John.17.4">Joh 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">24</reference>) was crucified. <div eID="gen33028" type="x-p"/>
entries.687b69c3825fac81ce45a9656bcee1dcb2d0280a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16776"/><div sID="gen33029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16776"/><hi type="bold">9. But--</hi>(it has happened) as it is written.<div eID="gen33029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eye hath not seen, &c.--</hi>Alford translates, "The things which eye saw not ... the things which God prepared ... to us God revealed through His Spirit." Thus, however, the "but" of <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference> is ignored. Rather construe, as Estius, "('We speak,' supplied from <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>), things which eye saw not (heretofore), ... things which God prepared ... But God revealed them to us," &c. The quotation is not a verbatim one, but an inspired exposition of the "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Is 64:4</reference>). The exceptive words, "O God, beside (that is, except) Thee," are not quoted directly, but are virtually expressed in the exposition of them (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>), "None but thou, O God, seest these mysteries, and God hath revealed them to us by His Spirit."<div eID="gen33030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entered--</hi>literally, "come up into the heart." A Hebraism (compare, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>, Margin). In <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Is 64:4</reference> it is "Prepared (literally, 'will do') for him that waiteth for Him"; here, "for them that love Him." For Isaiah spake to them who waited for Messiah's appearance as future; Paul, to them who love Him as having actually appeared (<reference osisRef="1John.4.19">1Jo 4:19</reference>); compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1Co 2:12</reference>, "the things that are freely given to us of God" <div eID="gen33031" type="x-p"/>
entries.028e754a2e3d62ccf25128b75f8a2f13dead7e3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16777"/><div sID="gen33032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16777"/><hi type="bold">10. revealed ... by ... Spirit--</hi>The inspiration of thoughts (so far as truth essential to salvation is concerned) makes the Christian (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Mt 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>, 27); that of words, the PROPHET (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2Sa 23:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.1">1Ki 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.5">5</reference>), "by the word of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13">1Co 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.30">Joh 20:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>). The secrets of revelation are secret to some, not because those who know them will not reveal them (for indeed, the very notion of revelation implies an unveiling of what had been veiled), but because those to whom they are announced have not the will or power to comprehend them. Hence the Spirit-taught alone know these secrets (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pr 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">15:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto us--</hi>the "perfect" or fully matured in Christian experience (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>). Intelligent men may understand the outline of doctrines; but without the Holy Spirit's revelation to the heart, these will be to them a mere outline--a skeleton, correct perhaps, but wanting life [Whatley, Cautions for the Times, 14], (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Lu 10:21</reference>).<div eID="gen33033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Spirit searcheth--</hi>working in us and with our spirits (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.16">Ro 8:16</reference>, 26, 27). The Old Testament shows us God (the Father) for us. The Gospels, God (the Son) with us. The Acts and Epistles, God (the Holy Ghost) in us [Monod], (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Ga 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen33034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deep things of God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.92.5">Psa 92:5</reference>). His divine nature, attributes, and counsels. The Spirit delights to explore the infinite depths of His own divine mind, and then reveal them to us, according as we are capable of understanding them (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">De 29:29</reference>). This proves the personality and Godhead of the Holy Ghost. Godhead cannot be separated from the Spirit of God, as manhood cannot be separated from the Spirit of man [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33035" type="x-p"/>
entries.d51d61a382f546cd77636700b5a5a310879c104f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16778"/><div sID="gen33036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16778"/><hi type="bold">11. what man, &c.--</hi>literally, "who of men knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of that man?"<div eID="gen33036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things of God knoweth no man--</hi>rather, "none knoweth," not angel or man. This proves the impossibility of any knowing the things of God, save by the Spirit of God (who alone knows them, since even in the case of man, so infinitely inferior in mind to God, none of his fellow men, but his own spirit alone knows the things hidden within him). <div eID="gen33037" type="x-p"/>
entries.13e5e28dcdc0f3272c9333e727413fb0a50c82c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16779"/><div sID="gen33038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16779"/><hi type="bold">12. we ... received, not ... spirit of ... world--</hi>the personal evil "spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>). This spirit is natural in the unregenerate, and needs not to be received.<div eID="gen33038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Spirit which is of God--</hi>that is, which comes from God. We have received it only by the gift of God, whose Spirit it is, whereas our own spirit is the spirit that is in us men (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1Co 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we might know ... things ... freely given ... of God--</hi>present experimental knowledge, to our unspeakable comfort, of His deep mysteries of wisdom, and of our future possession of the good "things which God hath prepared for them that love Him" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen33040" type="x-p"/>
entries.b46a9d7684f319db55925e6f1139cd806f6857b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16780"/><div sID="gen33041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16780"/><hi type="bold">13. also--</hi>We not only know by the Holy Ghost, but we also speak the "things freely given to us of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1Co 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which the Holy Ghost teacheth--</hi>The old manuscripts read "the Spirit" simply, without "Holy."<div eID="gen33042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comparing spiritual things with spiritual--</hi>expounding the Spirit-inspired Old Testament Scripture, by comparison with the Gospel which Jesus by the same Spirit revealed [Grotius]; and conversely illustrating the Gospel mysteries by comparing them with the Old Testament types [Chrysostom]. So the Greek word is translated, "comparing" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.12">2Co 10:12</reference>). Wahl (Key of the New Testament) translates, "explaining (as the Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.8">Ge 40:8</reference>, the Septuagint) to spiritual (that is, Spirit-taught) men, spiritual things (the things which we ourselves are taught by the Spirit)." Spirit-taught men alone can comprehend spiritual truths. This accords with <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">9, 10</reference>, 14, 15; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Co 3:1</reference>. Alford translates, "Putting together (combining) spirituals with spirituals"; that is, attaching spiritual words to spiritual things, which we should not do, if we were to use words of worldly wisdom to expound spiritual things (so <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">1Co 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>). Perhaps the generality of the neuters is designed to comprehend these several notions by implication. Comparing, or combining, spirituals with spirituals; implying both that spiritual things are only suited to spiritual persons (so "things" comprehended persons, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>), and also that spiritual truths can only be combined with spiritual (not worldly-wise) words; and lastly, spirituals of the Old and New Testaments can only be understood by mutual comparison or combination, not by combination with worldly "wisdom," or natural perceptions (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4-2Cor.1.9">2:1, 4-9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.119.18">Psa 119:18</reference>). <div eID="gen33043" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ca2cff901fc7734373e758c95050000619cb895: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16781"/><div sID="gen33044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16781"/><hi type="bold">14. natural man--</hi>literally, "a man of animal soul." As contrasted with the spiritual man, he is governed by the animal soul, which overbears his spirit, which latter is without the Spirit of God (Jude 19). So the animal (English Version, "natural") body, or body led by the lower animal nature (including both the mere human fallen reason and heart), is contrasted with the Spirit-quickened body (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44-1Cor.15.46">1Co 15:44-46</reference>). The carnal man (the man led by bodily appetites, and also by a self-exalting spirit, estranged from the divine life) is closely akin; so too the "earthly." "Devilish," or "demon-like"; "led by an evil spirit," is the awful character of such a one, in its worst type (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receiveth not--</hi>though they are offered to him, and are "worthy of being received by all men" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are foolishness unto him--</hi>whereas he seeks "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">1Co 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen33046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither can he--</hi>Not only does he not, but he cannot know them, and therefore has no wish to "receive" them (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Ro 8:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33047" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c36ea3cefb7e6e4863c505fac805460780d202e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16782"/><div sID="gen33048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16782"/><hi type="bold">15. He that is spiritual--</hi>literally, "the spiritual (man)." In <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>, it is "A [not 'the,' as English Version] natural man." The spiritual is the man distinguished above his fellow men, as he in whom the Spirit rules. In the unregenerate, the spirit which ought to be the organ of the Holy Spirit (and which is so in the regenerate), is overridden by the animal soul, and is in abeyance, so that such a one is never called "spiritual."<div eID="gen33048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgeth all things--</hi>and persons, by their true standard (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2-1Cor.6.4">1Co 6:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1Jo 4:1</reference>), in so far as he is spiritual. "Discerneth ... is discerned," would better accord with the translation of the same Greek (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>). Otherwise for "discerned," in <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>, translate, "judged of," to accord with the translation, "judgeth ... is judged" in this fifteenth verse. He has a practical insight into the verities of the Gospel, though he is not infallible on all theoretical points. If an individual may have the Spirit without being infallible, why may not the Church have the Spirit, and yet not be infallible (a refutation of the plea of Rome for the Church's infallibility, from <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>)? As the believer and the Church have the Spirit, and are yet not therefore impeccable, so he and the Church have the Spirit, and yet are not infallible or impeccable. He and the Church are both infallible and impeccable, only in proportion to the degree in which they are led by the Spirit. The Spirit leads into all truth and holiness; but His influence on believers and on the Church is as yet partial. Jesus alone, who had the Spirit without measure (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>), is both infallible and impeccable. Scripture, because it was written by men, who while writing were infallibly inspired, is unmixed truth (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.5">Pr 28:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1Jo 2:27</reference>). <div eID="gen33049" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa468c57cae449051e906aa34922e60af649b839: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16783"/><div sID="gen33050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16783"/><hi type="bold">16. For--</hi>proof of <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Co 2:15</reference>, that the spiritual man "is judged of no man." In order to judge the spiritual man, the ordinary man must "know the mind of the Lord." But "who of ordinary men knows" that?<div eID="gen33050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may instruct him--</hi>that is, so as to be able to set Him right as His counsellor (quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Is 40:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">14</reference>). So the Septuagint translates the Greek verb, which means to "prove," in <reference osisRef="Acts.9.22">Ac 9:22</reference>. Natural men who judge spiritual men, living according to the mind of God ("We have the mind of Christ"), are virtually wishing to instruct God, and bring Him to another mind, as counsellors setting to right their king.<div eID="gen33051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have the mind of Christ--</hi>in our degree of capability to apprehend it. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Is 40:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">14</reference> refers to Jehovah: therefore, as it is applied here to Christ, He is Jehovah. <chapter eID="1Cor.2"/>

entries.fc00207712ee6579315292bf852da553d8b3f6ae: <div eID="gen47314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen47315" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47316" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47316" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47315" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47317" type="x-p"/> The apostle makes an apology for his manner of preaching, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">1Cor 2:1</reference>. And gives the reason why he adopted that manner, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2-1Cor.2.5">1Cor 2:2-5</reference>. He shows that this preaching, notwithstanding it was not with excellence of human speech or wisdom, yet was the mysterious wisdom of God, which the princes of this world did not know, and which the Spirit of God alone could reveal, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.10">1Cor 2:6-10</reference>. It is the Spirit of God only that can reveal the things of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1Cor 2:11</reference>. The apostles of Christ know the things of God by the Spirit of God, and teach them, not in the words of man's wisdom, but in the words of that Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1Cor 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13">1Cor 2:13</reference>. The natural man cannot discern the things of the Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Cor 2:14</reference>. But the spiritual man can discern and teach them, because he has the mind of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Cor 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">1Cor 2:16</reference>. <div eID="gen47317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen47318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47319" type="x-p"/> When I came to you - Acting suitably to my mission, which was to preach the Gospel, but not with human eloquence, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">1Cor 1:17</reference>. I declared to you the testimony, the Gospel, of God, not with excellency of speech, not with arts of rhetoric, used by your own philosophers, where the excellence of the speech recommends the matter, and compensates for the want of solidity and truth: on the contrary, the testimony concerning Christ and his salvation is so supremely excellent, as to dignify any kind of language by which it may be conveyed. See the Introduction, Section 2.
entries.3cf012818bf865d7e84e149e3f1ac1b5bb59fb12: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen47319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47320" type="x-p"/> I determined not to know any thing among you - Satisfied that the Gospel of God could alone make you wise unto salvation, I determined to cultivate no other knowledge, and to teach nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, as the foundation of all true wisdom, piety, and happiness. No other doctrine shall I proclaim among you.
entries.8e01c0b0ccb168a5921b625c51583c8f83b2fb54: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen47320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47321" type="x-p"/> I was with you in weakness - It is very likely that St. Paul had not only something in his speech very unfavourable to a ready and powerful elocution, but also some infirmity of body that was still more disadvantageous to him. A fine appearance and a fine voice cover many weaknesses and defects, and strongly and forcibly recommend what is spoken, though not remarkable for depth of thought or solidity of reasoning. Many popular orators have little besides their persons and their voice to recommend them. Louis XIV. styled Peter du Bosc le plus beau parleur de son royaume, the finest speaker in his kingdom; and among his own people he was styled l'orateur parfait, the perfect orator. Look at the works of this French protestant divine, and you find it difficult to subscribe to the above sayings. The difficulty is solved by the information that the person of M. du Bosc was noble and princely, and his voice full, harmonious, and majestic. Paul had none of these advantages, and yet idolatry and superstition fell before him. Thus God was seen in the work, and the man was forgotten. <div eID="gen47321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47322" type="x-p"/> In fear, and in much trembling - This was often the state of his mind; dreading lest he should at any time be unfaithful, and so grieve the Spirit of God; or that, after having preached to others, himself should be a castaway. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">1Cor 9:27</reference>. <div eID="gen47322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47323" type="x-p"/> An eminent divine has said that it requires three things to make a good preacher; study, temptation, and prayer. The latter, no man that lives near to God can neglect; the former, no man who endeavors rightly to divide the word of truth will neglect; and with the second every man will be more or less exercised whose whole aim is to save souls. Those of a different cast the devil permits to pass quietly on in their own indolent and prayerless way.
entries.eb7222d0af54665208432f18101e29b3860acfbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen47323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47324" type="x-p"/> And my speech - Ὁ λογος μου, My doctrine; the matter of my preaching. <div eID="gen47324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47325" type="x-p"/> And my preaching - Το κηρυγμα μου, My proclamation, my manner of recommending the grand but simple truths of the Gospel. <div eID="gen47325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47326" type="x-p"/> Was not with enticing words of man's wisdom - Ενπειθοις ανθρωπινης σοφιας λογοις, With persuasive doctrines of human wisdom: in every case I left man out, that God might become the more evident. I used none of the means of which great orators avail themselves in order to become popular, and thereby to gain fame. <div eID="gen47326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47327" type="x-p"/> But in demonstration of the Spirit - Αποδειξει, In the manifestation; or, as two ancient MSS. have it, αποκαλυψει, in the revelation of the Spirit. The doctrine that he preached was revealed by the Spirit: that it was a revelation of the Spirit, the holiness, purity, and usefulness of the doctrine rendered manifest: and the overthrow of idolatry, and the conversion of souls, by the power and energy of the preaching, were the demonstration that all was Divine. The greater part of the best MSS., versions, and fathers, leave out the adjective ανθρωπινης, man's, before σοφιας, wisdom: it is possible that the word may be a gloss, but it is necessarily implied in the clause. Not with the persuasive discourses, or doctrines of wisdom; i.e. of human philosophy.
entries.89fc62cf7810a040d0ad733100b092b2aab6bf56: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen47327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47328" type="x-p"/> That your faith should not stand - That the illumination of your souls and your conversion to God might appear to have nothing human in it: your belief, therefore, of the truths which have been proposed to you is founded, not in human wisdom, but in Divine power: human wisdom was not employed; and human power, if it had been employed, could not have produced the change.
entries.578ddd033b37536681cf5f0a18bad9978c946442: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen47328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47329" type="x-p"/> We speak wisdom among them that are perfect - By the εν τοις τελειοις, among those that are perfect, we are to understand Christians of the highest knowledge and attainments- those who were fully instructed in the knowledge of God through Christ Jesus. Nothing, in the judgment of St. Paul, deserved the name of wisdom but this. And though he apologizes for his not coming to them with excellency of speech or wisdom, yet he means what was reputed wisdom among the Greeks, and which, in the sight of God, was mere folly when compared with that wisdom that came from above. Dr. Lightfoot thinks that the apostle mentions a fourfold wisdom. <div eID="gen47329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47330" type="x-p"/> 1. Heathen wisdom, or that of the Gentile philosophers, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">1Cor 1:22</reference>, which was termed by the Jews חכמה יונית chokmah yevanith, Grecian wisdom; and which was so undervalued by them, that they joined these two under the same curse: Cursed is he that breeds hogs; and cursed is he who teaches his son Grecian wisdom. Bava Kama, fol. 82. <div eID="gen47330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47331" type="x-p"/> 2. Jewish wisdom; that of the scribes and Pharisees, who crucified our Lord, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Cor 2:8</reference>. <div eID="gen47331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47332" type="x-p"/> 3. The Gospel, which is called the wisdom of God in a mystery, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Cor 2:7</reference>. <div eID="gen47332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47333" type="x-p"/> 4. The wisdom, του αιωνος τουτου, of this world; that system of knowledge which the Jews made up out of the writings of their scribes and doctors. This state is called העולם הזה haolam hazzeh, this or the present world; to distinguish it from העולם הבא haolam habba the world to come; i.e. the days of the Messiah. Whether we understand the term, this world, as relating to the state of the Gentiles, cultivated to the uttermost in philosophical learning, or the then state of the Jews, who had made the word of God of no effect by their traditions, which contained a sort of learning of which they were very fond and very proud, yet, by this Grecian and Jewish wisdom, no soul ever could have arrived at any such knowledge or wisdom as that communicated by the revelation of Christ. This was perfect wisdom; and they who were thoroughly instructed in it, and had received the grace of the Gospel, were termed τελειοι, the perfect. This, says the apostle, is not the wisdom of this world, for that has not the manifested Messiah in it; nor the wisdom of the rulers of this world - the chief men, whether philosophers among the Greeks, or rabbins among the Jews (for those we are to understand as implied in the term rulers, used here by the apostle) these rulers came to nought; for they, their wisdom, and their government, were shortly afterwards overturned in the destruction of Jerusalem. This declaration of the apostle is prophetic. The ruin of the Grecian superstition soon followed.
entries.ec331e22af4ea331e2af76303eb1da241ace9b6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen47333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47334" type="x-p"/> The wisdom of God in a mystery - The Gospel of Jesus Christ, which had been comparatively hidden from the foundation of the world, (the settling of the Jewish economy, as this phrase often means), though appointed from the beginning to be revealed in the fullness of time. For, though this Gospel was, in a certain sense, announced by the prophets, and prefigured by the law, yet it is certain that even the most intelligent of the Jewish rulers, their doctors, scribes, and Pharisees, had no adequate knowledge of it; therefore it was still a mystery to them and others, till it was so gloriously revealed by the preaching of the apostles.
entries.3304bd966c7cf88bdd5d4d78435921d5d6473a57: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen47334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47335" type="x-p"/> Which none of the princes of this world knew - Here it is evident that this world refers to the Jewish state, and to the degree of knowledge in that state: and the rulers, the priests, rabbins, etc., who were principally concerned in the crucifixion of our Lord. <div eID="gen47335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47336" type="x-p"/> The Lord of glory - Or the glorious Lord, infinitely transcending all the rulers of the universe; whose is eternal glory; who gave that glorious Gospel in which his followers may glory, as it affords them such cause of triumph as the heathens had not, who gloried in their philosophers. Here is a teacher who is come from God; who has taught the most glorious truths which it is possible for the soul of man to conceive; and has promised to lead all the followers of his crucified Master to that state of glory which is ineffable and eternal.
entries.8e53ff3248ba83a81aee389cdf7cf26cef9997c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen47336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47337" type="x-p"/> But, as it is written - The quotation is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference>. The sense is continued here from verse seven, and λαλουμεν, we speak, is understood - We do not speak or preach the wisdom of this world; but that mysterious wisdom of God, of which the prophet said: Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man the things which God has prepared for them that love him. These words have been applied to the state of glory in a future world; but they certainly belong to the present state, and express merely the wondrous light, life, and liberty which the Gospel communicates to them that believe in the Lord Jesus Christ in that way which the Gospel itself requires. To this the prophet himself refers; and it is evident, from the following verse, that the apostle also refers to the same thing. Such a scheme of salvation, in which God's glory and man's felicity should be equally secured, had never been seen, never heard of, nor could any mind but that of God have conceived the idea of so vast a project; nor could any power but his own have brought it to effect.
entries.125ea0099af54a612410e9c6ee41f6bc90e365c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen47337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47338" type="x-p"/> But God hath revealed them unto us - A manifest proof that the apostle speaks here of the glories of the Gospel, and not of the glories of the future world. <div eID="gen47338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47339" type="x-p"/> For the Spirit searcheth all things - This is the Spirit of God, which spoke by the prophets, and has now given to the apostles the fullness of that heavenly truth, of which He gave to the former only the outlines. <div eID="gen47339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47340" type="x-p"/> Yea, the deep things of God - It is only the Spirit of God which can reveal the counsels of God: these are the purposes which have existed in His infinite wisdom and goodness from eternity; and particularly what refers to creation, providence, redemption, and eternal glory, as far as men and angels are concerned in these purposes. The apostles were so fully convinced that the scheme of redemption proclaimed by the Gospel was Divine, that they boldly asserted that these things infinitely surpassed the wisdom and comprehension of man. God was now in a certain way become manifest; many attributes of his, which to the heathen world would have for ever lain in obscurity, (for the world by wisdom knew not God), were now not only brought to light as existing in him, but illustrated by the gracious displays which He had made of himself. It was the Spirit of God alone that could reveal these things; and it was the energy of that Spirit alone that could bring them all into effect - stamp and seal them as attributes and works of God for ever. The apostles were as truly conscious of their own inspiration as they were that they had consciousness at all; and what they spoke, they spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
entries.1dd228b4c292659a0483ae4185f19222f9fe18ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen47340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47341" type="x-p"/> For what man knoweth the things of a man - The word ανθρωπων in the first clause is omitted by the Codex Alexandrinus, and one other; and by Athanasius, Cyril, and Vigil of Tapsus. Bishop Pearce contends strongly against the authenticity of the word, and reads the passage thus: "For what is there that knoweth the things of a man, except the spirit of a man that is in him?" "I leave out," says the learned bishop, "ανθρωπων, with the Alexandrian MS., and read τις γαρ οιδεν τα του ανθρωπου; because I conceive that the common reading is wide of St. Paul's meaning; for to say, What man except the spirit of a man, is (I think) to speak improperly, and to suppose that the spirit of a man is a man; but it is very proper to say, What except the spirit of a man: τις is feminine as well as masculine, and therefore may be supplied with ουσια, or some such word, as well as with ανθρωπος." Though the authority for omitting this word is comparatively slender, yet it must be owned that its omission renders the text much more intelligible. But even one MS. may preserve the true reading. <div eID="gen47341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47342" type="x-p"/> The spirit of a man knows the things of a man: that is, a man is conscious of all the schemes, plans, and purposes, that pass in his own mind; and no man can know these things but himself. So, the Spirit of God, He whom we call the Third Person of the glorious Trinity, knows all the counsels and determinations of the Supreme Being. As the Spirit is here represented to live in God as the soul lives in the body of a man, and as this Spirit knows all the things of God, and had revealed those to the apostles which concern the salvation of the world, therefore what they spoke and preached was true, and men may implicitly depend upon it. The miracles which they did, in the name of Christ, were the proof that they had that Spirit, and spoke the truth of God.
entries.9b88a3cbff0b367c796a31d66a8cdc3c227f3016: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen47342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47343" type="x-p"/> Now we have received, not the spirit of the world - We, who are the genuine apostles of Christ, have received this Spirit of God, by which we know the deep things of God; and, through the teaching of that Spirit, we preach Christ crucified. We have not therefore received the spirit of the world - of the Jewish teachers, who are all looking for a worldly kingdom and a worldly Messiah, and interpret all the scriptures of the Old Testament which relate to Him in a carnal and worldly sense. <div eID="gen47343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47344" type="x-p"/> That we might know the things - We receive this teaching that we may know what those supereminently excellent things are which God has purposed freely to give to mankind. It is evident that, as the apostle means by princes of the world the rulers of the Jews, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.8">1Cor 2:6-8</reference>, so by spirit of the world he here means Jewish wisdom, or their carnal mode of interpreting the sacred oracles, and their carnal expectation of a worldly kingdom under the Messiah.
entries.11ce048b1bb2c756f728c0c8a207c32e9612be08: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen47344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47345" type="x-p"/> Which things also we speak - We dare no more use the language of the Jews and the Gentiles in speaking of those glorious things, than we can indulge their spirit. The Greek orators affected a high and florid language, full of tropes and figures, which dazzled more than it enlightened. The rabbins affected obscurity, and were studious to find out cabalistical meanings, which had no tendency to make the people wise unto salvation. The apostles could not follow any of these; they spoke the things of God in the words of God; every thing was plain and intelligible; every word well placed, clear, and nervous. He who has a spiritual mind will easily comprehend an apostle's preaching. <div eID="gen47345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47346" type="x-p"/> Comparing spiritual things with spiritual - This is commonly understood to mean, comparing the spiritual things under the Old Testament with the spiritual things under the New: but this does not appear to be the apostle's meaning. The word συγκρινοντες, which we translate comparing, rather signifies conferring, discussing, or explaining; and the word πνευματικοις should be rendered to spiritual men, and not be referred to spiritual things. The passage therefore should be thus translated: Explaining spiritual things to spiritual persons. And this sense the following verse absolutely requires.
entries.dd1d9be3194667065f0cc8fd4abfe8c01f77ffc4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen47346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47347" type="x-p"/> But the natural man - Ψυχικος, The animal man - the man who is in a mere state of nature, and lives under the influence of his animal passions; for the word ψυχη, which we often translate soul, means the lower and sensitive part of man, in opposition to νους, the understanding or rational part. The Latins use anima to signify these lower passions; and animus to signify the higher. The person in question is not only one who either has had no spiritual teaching, or has not profited by it; but one who lives for the present world, having no respect to spiritual or eternal things. This ψυχικος, or animal man, is opposed to the πνευματικος, or spiritual man: and, as this latter is one who is under the influence of the Spirit of God, so the former is one who is without that influence. <div eID="gen47347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47348" type="x-p"/> The apostle did speak of those high and sublime spiritual things to these animal men; but he explained them to those which were spiritual. He uses this word in this sense, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Cor 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1Cor 9:11</reference>; and particularly in <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Cor 2:15</reference> of the present chapter: He that is spiritual judgeth all things. <div eID="gen47348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47349" type="x-p"/> But the natural man - The apostle appears to give this - as a reason why he explained those deep spiritual things to spiritual men; because the animal man - the man who is in a state of nature, without the regenerating grace of the Spirit of God, receiveth not the things of the Spirit - neither apprehends nor comprehends them: he has no relish for them; he considers it the highest wisdom to live for this world. Therefore these spiritual things are foolishness to him; for while he is in his animal state he cannot see their excellency, because they are spiritually discerned, and he has no spiritual mind.
entries.3619e045081d06d97bee7e3fd1da421343c5fcbe: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen47349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47350" type="x-p"/> But he that is spiritual judgeth all things - He who has the mind of Christ discerns and judges of all things spiritual: yet he himself is not discerned by the mere animal man. Some suppose that the word ανακρινεται should be understood thus: He examines, scrutinizes, convinces, reproves, which it appears to mean in <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24">1Cor 14:24</reference>; and they read the verse thus: The spiritual man - the well-taught Christian, convinces, i.e. can easily convict, all men, (παντα, accusing), every animal man, of error and vice; yet he himself is convicted of no man; his mind is enlightened, and his life is holy; and therefore the animal man cannot convict him of sin. This is a good sense, but the first appears the most natural. See Pearce and Rosenmuller.
entries.f4263adef417dcf09e4dd2cdfe5faadc04ba18b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen47350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47351" type="x-p"/> For who hath known the mind of the Lord - Who that is still an animal man can know the mind of God? so as to instruct him, viz. the spiritual man, the same that is spoken of, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Cor 2:15</reference>. But the words may be better understood thus: How can the animal man know the mind of the Lord? and how can any man communicate that knowledge which he has never acquired, and which is foolishness to him, because it is spiritual, and he is animal? This quotation is made from <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Isa 40:13</reference>. <div eID="gen47351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47352" type="x-p"/> But we have the mind of Christ - He has endowed us with the same disposition, being born again by his Spirit; therefore we are capable of knowing his mind and receiving the teachings of his Spirit. These teachings we do receive, and therefore are well qualified to convey them to others. <div eID="gen47352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47353" type="x-p"/> The words, that he may instruct him, ὁς συμβιβασει αυτον, should be translated that he may teach It: that is, the mind of God; not instruct God, but teach his mind to others. And this interpretation the Hebrew will also bear. <div eID="gen47353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47354" type="x-p"/> Bishop Pearce observes: "The principal questions here are,, what συμβιβασει signifies, and what αυτον is relative to. The Hebrew word which the Septuagint translate by these two is יודיענו yodiennu: now, since ידיע yodia signifies as well to make known as to know, (and indeed this is the most frequent sense of it in the Old Testament), the suffix (postfix) נו nu, may relate to a thing, as well as to a person; and therefore it may be rendered not by him, but by it, i.e. the mind of the Lord.
